study.title: Joshua 6 The fall of Jericho and the faithfulness of the Lord
study.overview: Joshua 6 narrates Israel's first great conquest in Canaan: Jericho, a city closed and militarily prepared, is taken not by human strategy, but by obedience to an unusual divine order. The chapter highlights that the LORD had already delivered the city, but this promise required discipline, silence, march, trumpets and trust. The fall of the walls shows that victory comes from God; at the same time, the preservation of Rahab reveals mercy to those who believed and helped the messengers. The chapter ends by stating that the LORD was with Joshua, and this became visible to all.

outline.title: Jericho closed and the promise of victory
outline.explanation: The city is closed because of Israel, but the LORD declares to Joshua that Jericho has already been delivered. Divine instruction is alien to the standards of war: to surround the city, to to blews and to wait for the moment of God. The focus is less on military force and more in obedient confidence.

outline.title: The obedient march around the city
outline.explanation: Joshua send the orders to the priests, the armed men and the people. The ark of the covenant occupies the center of the procession, indicating that the advance of Israel depends on the presence of the LORD. The people must remain silent until the day of the cry, and the repetition of the march for six days tests patience and submission.

outline.title: The seventh day, the cry and the judgment on the city
outline.explanation: On the seventh day, the repeated culminates in the cry of the people and in the fall of the wall. Joshua recalls that the city is a thing consecrated to destruction, and that spoils cannot be taken for their own use. Total destruction expresses divine judgment upon Jericho, while silver, gold, and precious metals are separated into the treasure of the LORD.

outline.title: Raab spared and the name of Joshua released
outline.explanation: The spies carry out the oath made to Rahab, preserving it with his family. The city is burned, and Joshua pronounces a curse on any future attempt to rebuild it. The chapter concludes by saying that the LORD was with Joshua and that his fame spread throughout the land.

study.context: The text presents Jericho as a closed fortress in the face of Israel's approach. The notes point out that the city kept an important route to the interior of the earth, which helps to understand why its fall was decisive for Israel's campaign. The chapter also fits into the continuity of the speech that began before, when the Lord had encouraged Joshua with the promise of victory. The references to the spies and Rahab refer to the previous chapter, where she demonstrated faith in protecting the messengers. It is not necessary to assume more historical data than the chapter itself and the notes offer.
study.theology: This chapter teaches that the victory of God's people depends on the initiative and presence of God Himself, not of human superiority. The divine strategy subverts military logic: repeated marches, silence, trumpets and a final cry show that the battle belongs to the Lord. The ark at the centre of the procession symbolizes that the presence of God is the axis of conquest. The requirement not to take what has been consecrated to judgment reveals that victory does not authorize selfish appropriation; what God determines must be treated as holy. At the same time, the preservation of Rahab shows that God's mercy attains those who respond with faith and protection to the messengers. The chapter also highlights the leader's responsibility: Joshua faithfully communicates what he has received and the people must obey accurately. The outcome is the Lord with Joshua confirms that the success of his leadership comes from the company of God.

scholarViews.insight: The promise that the LORD had delivered Jericho strengthens Joshua, showing that his chief task was to obey what God had already guaranteed.
The march around the city tested the patient obedience of the people; the presence of the ark at the centre shows that the initiative was of the LORD, not of human strength.
The chapter describes Jericho as strongly closed and prepared to resist, which highlights the contrast between human defense and divine intervention in the fall of the walls.

questions: What most draws your attention: the strangeness of God's strategy or the patient obedience of Joshua and the people?
How does Rahab's preservation corrects the idea that God acts only with judgment, without mercy?
In what ways can the church today confuse human planning with real dependence on God's presence?
study.practice: Set aside time to examine in which areas you have sought results by force, haste or control, rather than simple obedience to what God has already ordained. Practice a faith that you can expect: stay faithful in the seemingly common repetitions, without despising the small steps that God commands you to take. It also reflects on the generosity of God to those who come from outside, like Rahab, and let it shape your way of welcoming and discerning people.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not explain all the symbolic details of the march, the trumpets or the fall of the walls; therefore, any more specific reading of these elements should be treated with caution. It is also not possible to safely affirm, from these sources, additional archaeological or chronological details about Jericho. Some expressions of the biblical text translate terms of judgment and consecration, but the exact scope of each formula should be read within the chapter itself.
